title: Spiritual Growth and Discipline
summary: How believers grow to maturity in Christ: the goal of growth, the spiritual disciplines, fellowship and service, and perseverance through dry seasons.
description: God wants every believer to grow "unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ" (Ephesians 4:13). This course explains the goal and stages of spiritual growth, the personal disciplines of the Word, meditation, prayer and solitude, the shared disciplines of worship, fellowship, service and giving, and how to keep growing through dryness, distraction and trials.
objectives: Explain the goal and stages of spiritual growth
Practise the disciplines of Bible reading, memorisation and meditation
Practise the disciplines of prayer, solitude, worship and fellowship
Identify common obstacles to growth and how to overcome them
outcomes: Set up a sustainable daily devotional habit
Explain why fellowship and service are needed for growth

modules.title: Growing Up in Christ
modules.intro: New birth is the start, not the finish. This week we see the goal and stages of growth.

lessons.title: The goal: Christlikeness
lessons.body:
God's purpose is that His children be "conformed to the image of his Son" (Romans 8:29). Paul laboured "that we may present every man perfect [mature] in Christ Jesus" (Colossians 1:28).

Maturity is not measured by years in church, titles, gifts or knowledge alone. It is seen in love, humility, holiness, wisdom and steady faith (Galatians 5:22-23; 2 Peter 1:5-8).

Peter commands, "grow in grace, and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ" (2 Peter 3:18). Growth is both a gift of grace and a calling to effort.

lessons.title: Stages of growth
lessons.body:
John writes to "little children", "young men" and "fathers" (1 John 2:12-14): new believers who know forgiveness, growing believers who are strong and overcome the evil one, and mature believers who know God deeply.

Peter tells new Christians, "As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby" (1 Peter 2:2). The writer of Hebrews rebukes believers who should be teachers but still need milk, not "strong meat" (Hebrews 5:12-14).

Growth is usually gradual, like a seed growing "first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn" (Mark 4:28).

lessons.title: God's work and ours
lessons.body:
Growth is God's work: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase" (1 Corinthians 3:6). It flows from abiding in Christ: "without me ye can do nothing" (John 15:5).

Yet we are told, "exercise thyself rather unto godliness" (1 Timothy 4:7). The word 'exercise' is from athletic training.

Spiritual disciplines are like a farmer's work: he cannot make the seed grow, but he ploughs, plants, waters and weeds so that growth can happen. The disciplines put us where God's grace works.

terms.def: The process of becoming more like Christ in character and understanding.
Christlike completeness, seen in love, holiness, wisdom and steady faith.
The basic teaching that nourishes new believers (1 Peter 2:2).
Deeper teaching for mature believers (Hebrews 5:14).
Remaining in close, dependent fellowship with Christ (John 15:4).
Habits such as Bible reading, prayer and fellowship through which God grows us.

texts.teaches: Paul laboured to present every man perfect in Christ.
As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word.
Strong meat belongs to those of full age.
Without Christ we can do nothing.
Exercise yourself unto godliness.

summary: The goal of growth is Christlikeness.
Believers grow through stages, from milk to strong meat.
God gives the growth as we abide in Christ.
Disciplines put us where grace works, like a farmer's labour.

questions.q: What is the goal of spiritual growth?
What do newborn believers need, according to 1 Peter 2:2?
options: The sincere milk of the word
A farmer's labour that allows growth

modules.title: Disciplines of the Word
modules.intro: God's Word is the main food for growth. This week we study reading, memorising and meditating on Scripture.

lessons.title: Reading the Bible regularly
lessons.body:
"Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God" (Matthew 4:4). The Bereans "searched the scriptures daily" (Acts 17:11).

Practical help:

- Choose a regular time and place.
- Use a reading plan: for example, a chapter of a Gospel and a psalm each day, or reading through the Bible in a year.
- Read with a question: what does this teach about God? About me? What should I do?
- Keep a simple notebook.

Audio Bibles help those who travel long hours or find reading hard. Faithfulness matters more than speed.

lessons.title: Memorising Scripture
lessons.body:
"Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee" (Psalm 119:11). Jesus answered each temptation in the wilderness with Scripture He knew by heart: "It is written" (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10).

Memorised Scripture helps in temptation, comfort, witnessing and prayer, even when no Bible is at hand.

Tips: start with short verses; learn the reference too; write verses on cards; review daily; memorise with a friend or family; sing Scripture songs. Choose verses about assurance (John 5:24), temptation (1 Corinthians 10:13), and the gospel (Romans 6:23).

lessons.title: Meditating on Scripture
lessons.body:
Biblical meditation is not emptying the mind but filling it with God's Word. The blessed man's "delight is in the law of the LORD; and in his law doth he meditate day and night. And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water" (Psalm 1:2-3).

To meditate is to chew slowly on a passage: read it several times, emphasise different words, ask questions, pray it back to God, and plan how to obey it.

God told Joshua to meditate "that thou mayest observe to do according to all that is written therein" (Joshua 1:8). The aim of meditation is obedience: "be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only" (James 1:22).

terms.def: A regular time set apart for Bible reading and prayer.
A schedule for reading through parts or all of the Bible.
Learning Scripture by heart.
Thinking deeply and prayerfully on Scripture in order to obey it.
Believers in Berea who searched the Scriptures daily (Acts 17:11).
Those who obey Scripture, not only hear it (James 1:22).

texts.teaches: Man lives by every word from the mouth of God.
God's word hidden in the heart guards against sin.
The blessed man meditates on God's law day and night.
Meditate on the book of the law in order to do it.
Be doers of the word, and not hearers only.

summary: Regular Bible reading is the believer's daily food.
Memorised Scripture guards against sin and helps in every situation.
Meditation fills the mind with God's Word.
The aim of all Bible intake is obedience.

questions.q: How did Jesus answer temptation in the wilderness?

options: Filling the mind with God's Word to obey it

modules.title: Disciplines Alone and Together
modules.intro: Growth needs both private devotion and the church. This week we study solitude, worship, fellowship, service and giving.

lessons.title: Solitude, silence and journaling
lessons.body:
Jesus often withdrew to lonely places to pray (Luke 5:16). He invited His tired disciples, "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while" (Mark 6:31).

In busy, noisy lives, especially with phones always near, believers need times of quiet: "Be still, and know that I am God" (Psalm 46:10).

Some find journaling helpful: writing prayers, lessons from Scripture, and God's answers. The Psalms themselves are like a journal of honest prayer. A weekly time of reflection, or a half-day retreat each month, can renew a weary heart.

lessons.title: Worship and fellowship
lessons.body:
We grow together. "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another" (Hebrews 10:25).

Corporate worship, hearing the Word preached, the Lord's Supper and prayer with others feed the soul (Acts 2:42). Small groups and house fellowships give room to ask questions, confess sins (James 5:16) and bear burdens (Galatians 6:2).

"Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend" (Proverbs 27:17). A Christian friend or mentor who asks honest questions is a great help to growth.

lessons.title: Service and giving
lessons.body:
We also grow by giving ourselves away. Jesus washed His disciples' feet and said, "If ye know these things, happy are ye if ye do them" (John 13:17). Using our gifts builds up others and matures us (1 Peter 4:10).

Giving loosens the grip of money on the heart: "where your treasure is, there will your heart be also" (Matthew 6:21). "God loveth a cheerful giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7).

Service should be humble and hidden, not for applause (Matthew 6:1-4). Start small: visiting the sick, helping in Sunday school, welcoming visitors, or teaching a younger believer.

terms.def: Time alone with God, away from crowds and noise.
Writing down prayers, reflections and lessons from God's Word.
Worshipping God together as a church.
A more mature believer who guides and encourages another.
Openness to others who help us keep our commitments.
One who gives freely and gladly (2 Corinthians 9:7).

texts.teaches: Come apart into a desert place and rest a while.
Be still, and know that I am God.
Do not forsake assembling together; exhort one another.
Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend.
Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

summary: Solitude and silence renew the heart in a noisy world.
Corporate worship and fellowship are essential to growth.
Service and giving shape the heart toward Christ.

options: Come apart and rest a while

modules.title: Keep Growing
modules.intro: Every believer faces seasons of dryness and obstacles. This week we study how to keep growing for a lifetime.

lessons.title: Obstacles to growth
lessons.body:
Jesus' parable of the sower names three obstacles (Mark 4:15-19):

- **Satan** snatching away the Word.
- **Shallowness**: no root, so trials make people stumble.
- **Thorns**: "the cares of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts of other things" choking the Word.

Other obstacles include unconfessed sin, bitterness (Hebrews 12:15), laziness (Proverbs 24:30-34), and isolation from other believers.

The remedy is to deal honestly with each: resist the devil, put down roots, weed out thorns, and return to fellowship.

lessons.title: Dry seasons and trials
lessons.body:
Mature believers also know dry seasons. David cried, "My soul thirsteth for thee... in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is" (Psalm 63:1). Asaph nearly slipped when he envied the wicked, until he "went into the sanctuary of God" (Psalm 73:2, 17).

Trials are part of growth: "the trying of your faith worketh patience. But let patience have her perfect work, that ye may be perfect and entire" (James 1:3-4).

In dry times, keep the disciplines going even when feelings are weak, be honest with God in lament, seek counsel, and remember God's past faithfulness (Psalm 77:11).

lessons.title: A rule of life
lessons.body:
A **rule of life** is a simple plan for the habits that keep you close to God. It might include:

- **Daily**: Bible reading, prayer, a verse to memorise.
- **Weekly**: Lord's Day worship, house fellowship, one act of service.
- **Monthly**: a half-day of reflection, a day of fasting, time with a mentor.
- **Yearly**: a retreat, reading through a book of the Bible in depth.

Keep it realistic and review it every few months. Paul's goal was simple: "forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark" (Philippians 3:13-14).

terms.def: The cares, riches and desires that choke the Word (Mark 4:19).
Resentment that springs up and troubles many (Hebrews 12:15).
A season when God feels distant and devotion feels hard.
Steadfast endurance that trials produce (James 1:3).
A simple personal plan of daily, weekly, monthly and yearly habits for growth.
Paul's picture of steady progress toward Christlikeness (Philippians 3:14).

texts.teaches: Cares, riches and lusts choke the word.
Let no root of bitterness spring up and trouble you.
My soul thirsts for God in a dry and thirsty land.
The trying of your faith works patience.
I press toward the mark for the prize of God's high calling.

summary: The parable of the sower names Satan, shallowness and thorns as obstacles.
Bitterness, laziness and isolation also hinder growth.
Dry seasons and trials can deepen faith.
A simple rule of life keeps us growing for a lifetime.

questions.q: What chokes the Word in the parable of the sower?

options: Went into the sanctuary of God

questions.q: What does the trying of faith produce?

short.q: What is the goal of spiritual growth?
short.model: To be conformed to the image of Christ and become mature in Him.

short.q: Explain how growth is both God's work and ours.
short.model: God gives the increase as we abide in Christ, yet we exercise ourselves through disciplines that put us where grace works, like a farmer.

short.q: Give three benefits of memorising Scripture.
short.model: It guards against sin in temptation, gives comfort, and equips for witness and prayer.

short.q: What is biblical meditation and what is its aim?
short.model: Thinking deeply and prayerfully on Scripture, with the aim of obeying it.

short.q: Why is fellowship necessary for growth?
short.model: Believers exhort and sharpen one another, confess sins and bear burdens; we are told not to forsake assembling (Hebrews 10:25).

short.q: How should a believer respond to spiritual dryness?
short.model: Keep up the disciplines even when feelings are weak, pray honestly in lament, seek counsel and remember God's faithfulness.

lists.q: List three obstacles to growth from the parable of the sower.
List four shared or outward disciplines.

assignments.title: My rule of life
assignments.prompt: Write a personal rule of life with daily, weekly, monthly and yearly habits. Explain the biblical reason for each habit using passages from this course, and describe how you will keep it realistic.

assignments.title: Meditating on a psalm
assignments.prompt: Meditate on Psalm 1 or Psalm 63 for one week. Describe how you meditated, what you learned about God and yourself, and two specific steps of obedience that came from it.
